name: Minimally invasive plate osteosynthesis approach to the clavicle
corridor: Two short end incisions joined by a blunt epiperiosteal tunnel for anterior or superior bridge plating

positioning.text: Position beach-chair or supine with the scapula supported and the arm mobile to restore clavicular length and alignment indirectly.

setup.text: Template plate length and location before incision, prep the entire clavicle and arm, and ensure continuous fluoroscopic visualization of both ends and the fracture.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark both clavicular ends, fracture zone, planned plate ends and holes, sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints, and supraclavicular nerve territory.

incision.text: Make separate medial and lateral incisions approximately 2–3 cm long over the planned plate ends, adding only targeted stab incisions for screws or reduction tools.

superficial_interval.text: Protect visible supraclavicular branches, open fascia locally, and create a blunt subcutaneous or epiperiosteal tunnel connecting the end windows.

deep_interval.text: Pass the plate through the prepared tunnel without stripping the fracture zone, using a small direct fracture window only if indirect reduction fails.

layers.text: Skin and subcutaneous tissue at two windows, supraclavicular nerve branches, local fascia and periosteum, blunt tunnel, then main clavicular fragments.

structures_encountered.text: Supraclavicular nerves, platysma, clavipectoral fascia, periosteum and the medial and lateral main fragments are encountered; intermediate fragments remain covered.

structures_at_risk.text: Supraclavicular nerves, subclavian vessels, brachial plexus, pleura, and skin over the tunneled plate are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Tunnel and drill under controlled contact with bone; never pass instruments blindly deep to the clavicle or across the medial-middle junction.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid forceful retraction through short incisions, which can injure sensory branches or skin; extend a window when visualization is inadequate.

exposure.text: Exposes the main fragments and plate endpoints while preserving fracture hematoma and soft-tissue attachments around comminution.

limitations.text: Indirect reduction makes length, axis, and rotation harder to judge and is poorly suited when anatomic reduction of a simple fracture or direct debridement is essential.

extensions.text: Add a limited fracture-site incision for a blocking fragment or irreducible deformity, or convert to the full open approach when safe reduction cannot be verified.

indications.text: Best suited to selected multifragmentary midshaft fractures where relative stability and biologic preservation are desired; some simple patterns may qualify when soft-tissue considerations favor MIPO.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid for medial or lateral patterns outside the implant design, gross contamination, neurovascular exploration, or a simple pattern requiring direct anatomic compression when indirect control is unreliable.

implant_implications.text: Use a sufficiently long bridge plate with balanced fixation in both main fragments, confirm plate centering, and protect deep structures during every percutaneous screw pass.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Imaging must confirm clavicular length, coronal and sagittal alignment, rotation, plate location, endpoint fixation, and safe screw lengths.

closure.text: Close each fascial window securely over the plate, incorporating preserved periosteum when possible, then close skin without tension.

complications.text: Complications include malalignment or shortening, supraclavicular numbness, vascular or plexus injury, pneumothorax, infection, nonunion, implant failure or prominence, and skin compromise.

bailouts.text: If fluoroscopy cannot prove length and rotation or the plate cannot pass safely, open the fracture deliberately rather than persisting with blind tunneling.

procedure_applications.condition: A midshaft fracture is suitable for indirect reduction and bridge plating with preservation of intermediate fragments

questions.question: How many principal incisions are used for clavicle MIPO?
questions.answer: Two short incisions over the medial and lateral plate ends.

questions.question: What biology does MIPO preserve?
questions.answer: Fracture hematoma and soft-tissue attachments to intermediate fragments.

questions.question: Which reduction parameters must be verified indirectly?
